title: Video-rate cellular imaging through living tissue

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a microscope that produces sustained, cellular-resolution three-dimensional images several millimeters beneath the surface of living tissue while blood flows and the tissue moves. Illumination and detection would operate from the same side, in reflection geometry, without requiring transmission through a thin specimen. The goal is to recover cellular structure and dynamics despite strong scattering that scrambles the paths of incoming and returning light.

As a proposed scope definition, the system would form video-rate volumes while maintaining cellular resolution and stable field coverage for minutes. It would require neither an implanted focal light source nor an externally imposed guide star, such as an ultrasound-defined reference used to identify light paths. Whether endogenous tissue features or image-derived feedback may serve as internal references must be declared explicitly. Avoiding an implanted point source alone is a weaker requirement than guide-star-free operation.

The advance could involve adaptive correction, wavefront shaping, computational reconstruction, or a combination of these. These approaches can have different outputs: reconstructing an image from scattered measurements does not necessarily create a sharp physical light focus inside the tissue. The central imaging capability should therefore be evaluated separately from any additional claim of controlled deep light delivery.

significance.text: If demonstrated, this capability would substantially extend direct optical observation of cellular structure and activity in their living environment. Optical measurements offer contrast from fluorescence, absorption, scattering and Raman scattering, among other mechanisms. Sustained access to these signals at several-millimeter depths could expose relationships between cells, blood vessels and surrounding tissue that are difficult to observe at comparable depth, resolution and speed with the documented optical methods. The benefit depends on the contrast actually measured; cellular spatial resolution alone does not establish molecular specificity.

Deep functional imaging would be a direct downstream possibility where suitable labels or endogenous contrast, sufficient photon counts and adequate temporal sampling are available. Clinical optical biopsy would additionally require evidence that the images support reliable diagnosis in the intended patients and tissues. Therapeutic light delivery would require a physical focus or other controlled illumination pattern, adequate dose and demonstrated safety. Computational recovery of an image does not by itself establish any of those therapeutic capabilities.

Making tissue locally transparent is a useful metaphor for this bounded imaging advance, but it would not mean literal transparency across wavelengths, contrast mechanisms or organs. Scattering correction cannot restore photons lost to absorption. The supplied multiphoton feature emphasizes the tradeoff between scattering and absorption and notes the importance of water absorption above 1.2 µm. Several-millimeter local imaging therefore does not establish centimeter-scale human imaging or whole-organ optical transparency, and the supplied evidence does not set a universal human penetration limit.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is sustained cellular image formation through strong, rapidly changing scattering at depth, with access from one side and without an external guide star. Conventional high-resolution optical imaging is often confined to superficial tissue, while multiphoton microscopy extends useful imaging into the millimeter range. Neither a universal fraction-of-a-millimeter scattering cutoff nor a universal one-millisecond motion timescale describes all tissues and wavelengths.

A central engineering barrier is completing the optical measurement, calculation and correction before tissue motion invalidates the measured scattering pattern. In the reviewed 2017 mouse-brain experiment, decorrelation became faster with source depth, reaching sub-millisecond times at the deepest measured location. Computational methods face a related constraint: scattering-matrix measurements must be completed before the arrangement of scatterers changes substantially. High spatial control is consequently insufficient unless acquisition and feedback also keep pace with the tissue.

Multiphoton microscopy suppresses background by confining nonlinear excitation, but it still depends on ballistic excitation photons reaching the focus. Emitted fluorescence can scatter on its return path and remain useful because its origin was localized during excitation. This distinction matters: the limitation is not that every detected photon must remain unscattered. At increasing depth, maintaining useful excitation, adequate signal relative to background and sufficient photon counts at high volume rates remains difficult, while absorption imposes losses that wavefront correction cannot undo.

Engineering synthesis: the proposed system must combine depth, resolution, volume size, acquisition speed and exposure limits in the same living preparation. A convincing solution must avoid trading away most of the field, slowing acquisition below the tissue dynamics, or relying on a guide-star geometry unavailable in the intended specimen. The supplied examples demonstrate important components of this challenge, but their reported performance figures cannot be combined into a single demonstrated system.

current_state.text: Qureshi, Brake and colleagues reported in Biomedical Optics Express in October 2017 that mean speckle decorrelation times were 7.5, 3.5, 1.1 and 0.6 ms at source depths of 1.1, 1.8, 2.5 and 3.2 mm, respectively. The experiment used 632.8-nm illumination, anesthetized mice, a craniotomy and an inserted fiber source. These results establish rapid dynamics in that preparation, rather than a universal timescale for visible and near-infrared imaging in living tissue. The authors estimated that then-current wavefront shaping with approximately 3 ms latency could access roughly 1–2 mm depth; this was a historical estimate, not a November 2026 performance ceiling.

Aaron K. LaViolette and Chris Xu’s April 2025 Optics & Photonics News feature reports in vivo mouse-brain vasculature imaging beyond 2 mm and neuronal activity imaging beyond 1 mm at approximately 10 Hz. These reports show that a blanket first-millimeter limit on cellular or functional optical imaging is too restrictive. They do not establish cellular-resolution volumes several millimeters deep at video rate, and the separate depth and temporal-resolution statements should not be treated as simultaneous performance in one experiment.

The research notes attribute to Chris Xu’s August 2024 Cell review a projected three-photon signal-to-background limit of approximately 3–4 mm for mouse-brain vasculature, described as nearly twice the deepest imaging then demonstrated. The supplied evidence review could not verify either quantitative statement because the retained page contained only a redirect. These figures remain unverified attributions, rather than established limits or demonstrated depths in this record. The access limitation does not establish that the attributed statements are false.

Luo and colleagues’ Science Advances paper, identified as a 2022 publication in the supplied review, reports 518,400 independent controls, an 8.1 ms system runtime and 5.5 ms latency for time-reversed ultrasonically encoded optical focusing. Independent controls should not be equated without qualification to the number of effective optical modes. In its live-zebrafish demonstration, an ultrasonic guide star lay in a water tank between the fish and a ground-glass diffuser, with a speckle correlation time of about 46 ms. This demonstrates rapid guided focusing through dynamic scattering media; it does not demonstrate guide-star-free cellular imaging inside mammalian tissue. The review had the main article, but not its separately referenced supplement.

Zhang and colleagues’ scattering-matrix tomography manuscript reports reflection-mode imaging of a resolution target beneath a 0.98-mm-thick slice of ex vivo mouse-brain tissue. This is imaging through brain tissue to an underlying target, rather than cellular volumetric imaging within a living brain. The retained manuscript reports approximately three minutes for acquisition and minutes to hours for processing, which does not meet the proposed moving-tissue video benchmark. The supplied review assessed manuscript text without independent figure inspection; referenced supplementary material was not included.

The scattering-matrix tomography work is available as arXiv:2306.08793, and its retained landing page lists a 2025 journal reference, Advanced Photonics 7, 046008, with related DOI 10.1117/1.AP.7.4.046008. This corrects the earlier statement that journal publication was unconfirmed in the retained record. The journal version itself was not inspected in the supplied review, so the performance description above remains tied to the reviewed manuscript.

Evidence boundary: the supplied record documents these historical achievements and limitations, but contains no bounded freshness-search record establishing coverage through November 1, 2026. It therefore neither establishes that the complete proposed capability has been achieved nor proves that it remains unachieved at that date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed primary demonstration: acquire cellular-resolution three-dimensional volumes several millimeters below the surface of a living mammalian brain or comparably scattering organ, with blood flow present and illumination and detection from the same side. Declare the numerical volume frequency intended by video rate, the volume dimensions, usable field coverage, depth reference, and lateral and axial resolution. Demonstrate those properties together in one preparation, with stable resolution and coverage for minutes. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not published consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained cellular-resolution volumes several millimeters deep in living tissue

completion_criteria.text: Proposed access and reference requirements: state precisely what intact surface includes, including whether skin, skull or other overlying structures remain present and whether any surgical window is used. Show that no implanted focal source or externally imposed guide star supplies the needed reference. Declare any endogenous reference, fluorescent labeling or image-based feedback so that the meaning of guide-star-free operation is reproducible.
completion_criteria.label: Document tissue access and references for reproducible guide-star-free operation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement and safety requirements: report the entire acquisition-to-image delay, including calibration, scanning, reconstruction and correction updates, alongside tissue motion and decorrelation conditions. Quantify signal relative to background and validate cell-scale image fidelity against an independent reference where feasible. For systems claiming diffraction-limited focusing, measure focal performance separately from reconstructed image resolution. Report wavelength, incident power, exposure duration, heating and photodamage assessments under the actual volumetric acquisition conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Report acquisition-to-image delay, image fidelity, and volumetric acquisition safety

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat the combined demonstration across multiple animals or specimens and seek independent replication with sufficiently documented hardware, algorithms and acquisition settings. Report failure conditions across the tested depths, tissue types, motion levels and contrast mechanisms. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not universal operation in every tissue or wavelength. Centimeter-scale human imaging and therapeutic light delivery would remain separate claims requiring their own evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Repeat demonstrations across specimens and document replication methods and limits

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with OPT-07, Macroscopic programmable visible optical aperture: a programmable aperture could supply the spatial optical control used in wavefront shaping. OPT-05 additionally requires learning or compensating the changing tissue response and producing useful images at depth. A large controllable aperture alone does not demonstrate that imaging capability.

Conceptual comparison with OPT-06, Practical visible far-field super-resolution optic: both concern improved optical access to fine spatial detail, but the stated goals differ. OPT-06 targets super-resolution optics, whereas OPT-05 targets cellular imaging through strong, moving tissue scattering. OPT-05 can be transformative at ordinary diffraction-limited cellular resolution without demonstrating super-resolution.

Conceptual comparison with OPT-10, Room-temperature short-wave-infrared photon-counting cameras: sensitive detection could be an enabling component for photon-limited deep imaging where the wavelengths and contrast are compatible. A camera alone does not restore absorbed photons, establish a deep excitation focus or solve rapidly changing scattering. Conversely, OPT-05 does not require that a particular room-temperature detector innovation be achieved.

Conceptual comparison with the remaining roster entries: OPT-01, Cascadable few-photon optical transistor, and OPT-02, Arrays of deterministic single-photon sources above the loss threshold, target optical switching and photon generation. OPT-03, Room-temperature, electrically pumped laser grown in a silicon CMOS flow, and OPT-09, Few-femtojoule optical links inside computing packages, target integrated sources and communications. OPT-04, Laboratory-scale coherent hard X-ray source, concerns a different source and wavelength regime, while OPT-08, The quantum vacuum as a laboratory nonlinear optical medium, concerns a different physical interaction. None of these stated identities entails OPT-05’s living-tissue imaging capability, and they remain separate innovations. These distinctions are based on the supplied titles rather than fuller technical records.

Adaptive optics, wavefront shaping, multiphoton microscopy and reflection-matrix imaging are related approaches that address different portions of OPT-05. Multiphoton excitation confines signal generation; wavefront shaping controls propagation; reflection-matrix methods can reconstruct images computationally from scattered measurements. Their overlap does not erase the distinction between a physical focus, an image reconstructed after acquisition and sustained volumetric imaging in living tissue.

Based only on the supplied description, historical item 5—a universal adaptive-optics corrector for any aperture and wavelength—overlaps OPT-05 where adaptive correction is applied to tissue scattering. OPT-05 has a narrower application domain but demands image formation in strongly scattering, rapidly changing living tissue. The historical item’s original text was not supplied, so the comparison remains conceptual; a detailed contrast with astronomical adaptive optics cannot be established from this record.

change_log.change: Preserved OPT-05’s identity while making its proposed reflection-mode, volumetric, moving-tissue capability explicit.
change_log.reason: The innovation is a coherent combined imaging goal even though some supporting assertions require qualification.

change_log.change: Replaced universal depth and motion cutoffs with tissue-dependent statements and the 2017 experiment’s full depth–decorrelation measurements and preparation.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports specific mouse-brain measurements, not a universal visible or near-infrared tissue limit.

change_log.change: Distinguished ballistic multiphoton excitation from collection of scattered emitted fluorescence.
change_log.reason: The earlier unscattered-fraction wording incorrectly extended the excitation restriction to useful detected emission.

change_log.change: Retained the attributed 2024 Cell estimates as explicitly unverified figures.
change_log.reason: The retained source contained only a redirect; lack of usable access neither verifies nor disproves the numerical claims.

change_log.change: Added the 2025 feature’s reported imaging depths and approximately 10 Hz neuronal-activity sampling without combining them into a single volumetric result.
change_log.reason: These reports correct the first-millimeter generalization but do not establish the full proposed capability.

change_log.change: Corrected the time-reversal focusing account with authorship, publication year, 518,400 independent controls, runtime, latency and experimental geometry.
change_log.reason: The supplied review had the main article and distinguished independent controls from effective modes, guided focusing from imaging, and a focus between scattering layers from one inside living tissue.

change_log.change: Corrected scattering-matrix tomography to a target beneath 0.98 mm of ex vivo tissue, added acquisition and processing times, and acknowledged the listed 2025 journal publication.
change_log.reason: The retained evidence does not show living-brain volumes and contradicts the earlier statement that journal publication was unconfirmed.

change_log.change: Separated direct imaging benefits from conditional functional, diagnostic and therapeutic applications.
change_log.reason: Contrast availability, diagnostic validity and physical therapeutic focusing require additional evidence beyond computational image formation.

change_log.change: Bounded the local-transparency analogy and removed the categorical comparison with other medical imaging modalities.
change_log.reason: Absorption remains a separate constraint, and the supplied sources do not substantiate the original broad comparison.

change_log.change: Expanded completion proposals to define volume frequency, anatomy, resolution, reference sources, exposure, reproducibility and failure boundaries.
change_log.reason: The proposed demonstration needs measurable conditions without presenting those conditions as consensus standards or universal proof.

change_log.change: Added explicit roster distinctions and retained the historical adaptive-optics comparison with a provenance limitation.
change_log.reason: Related enabling components and overlapping methods should remain separate concepts; only a description of the historical item was supplied.

change_log.change: Preserved the freshness, journal-version, supplementary-material and figure-inspection limitations.
change_log.reason: The final account must reflect the supplied review’s evidence boundaries without implying additional document inspection or current literature coverage.

unresolved_issues: Whether the complete proposed capability had been demonstrated by November 1, 2026 remains unknown because no bounded freshness-search record was supplied.

The attributed 2024 Cell review estimates of a 3–4 mm three-photon signal-to-background limit and a nearly twofold gap over demonstrated depth remain unverified because the retained page was only a redirect.
Guide-star-free operation needs an agreed definition, especially concerning endogenous references, image-based feedback and externally imposed nonimplanted guide stars.
The proposed benchmark still needs numerical volume frequency, volume dimensions, resolution targets, anatomical access conditions and acceptable exposure limits.
The listed 2025 scattering-matrix tomography journal version was not inspected; differences from the reviewed manuscript remain unknown.

The supplied review did not include the separately referenced supplementary materials for the time-reversal focusing and scattering-matrix tomography papers, and did not independently inspect the latter’s figures.
The original text and supporting evidence for historical item 5 were not supplied, limiting the adaptive-optics comparison.
The practical absorption-limited depth in particular human tissues is not quantified by the supplied evidence.

brief.title: Live views of cells deep inside living tissue
possible: Researchers could watch individual cells several millimeters inside living tissue as blood flows and the tissue moves. A microscope would capture three-dimensional views at video speed for minutes, sending light in and collecting it from the same side.
why: This would let scientists observe cells, blood vessels and surrounding tissue together in their living environment. They could study relationships that are difficult to see at this depth, detail and speed.

sources.who: Muhammad Mohsin Qureshi, Joshua Brake and colleagues
sources.showed: This experimental study examines how quickly scattered-light patterns change at different depths in living mouse brains.
sources.cited_for: Tissue motion sets a deadline for measuring and correcting scattered light.
sources.not_established: Measuring changing light patterns does not establish deep cellular imaging.

sources.who: Muhammad Mohsin Qureshi, Joshua Brake and colleagues
sources.showed: The team measured increasingly rapid changes in scattered-light patterns deeper in living mouse brains, using an inserted light source.
sources.cited_for: Corrections must keep pace with blood flow and tissue motion.
sources.not_established: The experiment measured light scattering rather than producing cellular images without an implanted source.

sources.showed: This review discusses deep imaging using three-photon microscopy, which combines light particles to excite light-emitting labels.
sources.cited_for: The review addresses projected depth limits for deep optical imaging.
sources.not_established: A projected depth limit does not demonstrate sustained cellular imaging at video speed.

sources.who: Aaron K. LaViolette and Chris Xu
sources.showed: Their review reports imaging blood vessels beyond 2 mm in living mouse brains. It also describes deep recordings of nerve-cell activity.
sources.quote: Currently, the signal strength rather than SBR limits the depth of three-photon imaging.
sources.cited_for: Existing optical methods already reach deep brain structures, while balancing depth, speed and signal strength.
sources.not_established: The reported depths and activity-recording speeds do not establish the full capability together.

sources.showed: The team rapidly focused light between a living zebrafish and a light-scattering screen. Ultrasound supplied a reference that helped identify the light paths.
sources.quote: With this technique, we demonstrate in vivo light focusing in between a highly opaque adult zebrafish of 5.1 millimeters in thickness and a ground glass diffuser.
sources.cited_for: Light can be focused rapidly through changing, strongly scattering material with an external reference.
sources.not_established: The focus was outside the fish, and the experiment required an ultrasound reference.

sources.who: Yiwen Zhang, Minh Dinh and colleagues
sources.showed: The team computationally recovered images of a test target beneath roughly 1 mm of removed mouse-brain tissue, with light entering and returning from the same side.
sources.quote: We synthesize conventional reflection-based methods (RCM, OCT, and OCM) and the most advanced matrix-based method VRM, and found all of them to fail at these depths.
sources.cited_for: Computation can recover detailed images despite strong light scattering.
sources.not_established: Imaging a target beneath removed tissue does not demonstrate fast cellular imaging within moving, living tissue.

shown: Existing methods demonstrate separate parts of the goal. LaViolette and Xu describe deep imaging in living mouse brains. Luo’s team demonstrated rapid guided focusing, while Zhang’s team recovered images through removed brain tissue. These results have not established the combined capability.
missing: A sustained demonstration must combine depth, cellular detail, video-speed volumes and stable coverage in the same living tissue.
The system must work from one side without an implanted light source or an externally imposed reference.
Measurements and corrections must keep pace with tissue motion while collecting enough light without damaging tissue.
The combined result needs repeat demonstrations across specimens and independent replication.

milestones.label: Sustained deep views of living cells at video speed
milestones.explanation: A microscope would have to sustain cellular-detail volumes several millimeters deep in a living organ, with blood flowing and access from one side. Depth, speed, volume size and coverage must hold together for minutes.

milestones.label: Reproducible operation without an external reference
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to specify surgical access and show operation without implanted light sources or external reference signals, called guide stars. Any tissue-based references, labels or image feedback must be stated.

milestones.label: Measured image delay, accuracy and tissue safety
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to measure total image delay, cellular accuracy, background light and tissue damage under actual scanning conditions, assessing any claimed physical focus separately. This establishes whether the views are timely, faithful and safe.

milestones.label: Repeated results with clear operating limits
milestones.explanation: The combined result would have to recur across specimens, with methods detailed enough for independent replication and failures reported. This establishes where the microscope works and where it stops working.

uncertain: The required video speed, volume size, cellular detail and acceptable light exposure still need numerical definitions.
Whether tissue features or image feedback count as permitted internal references remains unsettled.
How deeply useful images can reach before absorption removes too much light remains tissue-dependent.
